# AI workflow automation services for cross-system work

Wexpro Labs maps and pilots recurring business workflows across browser and desktop software, including legacy systems without suitable APIs.

## Direct answer

Start with one recurring process. Map the applications, handoffs, checks, exceptions, and judgment points in one representative case. Define eligible cases and the evidence that proves completion, then run a controlled pilot against thresholds agreed before volume increases.

## The problem

Many operational processes still require a person to carry information between inboxes, documents, portals, spreadsheets, and desktop applications. A workflow can be repeatable even when the systems do not share one complete API path.

## Map, review, measure

1. Map: name the workflow, define the intended result, and demonstrate one representative case across the software it actually uses.
2. Review: inspect the mapped steps, define exceptions, and assign consequential actions that require human approval or judgment.
3. Measure: pilot only the agreed eligible cases and report verified completions, no-touch completions, exception-review time, runtime, and cost.

## Horizontal fit

Strong first workflows repeat often, cross multiple systems, follow known checks, include a routine path, and end in an observable result. Examples include request intake, reconciliation, reporting, record changes, onboarding, and recurring checks.

## Team hours returned

The manual baseline establishes the active team time required for one case. The pilot measures eligible cases, verified no-touch completions, and time spent reviewing exceptions.

Estimated routine team hours returned = (active manual minutes per case × verified no-touch completions − exception review minutes) ÷ 60.

Automated elapsed runtime is reported separately because it affects throughput but does not consume team labor when the run is unattended.

## Controlled pilot

Start with one recurring process. Define the result, map the real work, assign the human checks, and compare completion, runtime, review burden, cost, and team hours returned with the current process. Agree on quality, coverage, safety, labor, and cost thresholds before the pilot begins.
